summary: The University of Illinois Center for Advanced Computation proposes graphic display modes for its ARPANET node. Unlike other nodes, it was setting up a system for the ILLIAC IV and the network, so it was building its graphics system from scratch.

plainLanguage.summary: A new lab that was not simply plugging an old computer into the network says what picture modes it wants to support.

questions: what graphic display modes did illinois propose
why was the illinois node different
subtitle: Display modes for computer graphics over the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The University of Illinois was building a new ARPANET node with graphics capabilities from scratch, and needed to define what display modes the network graphics protocol should support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes eight standard display element types (points, lines, vectors, character streams, viewport, transformations, equipment-specific data, and input readback) and four new grey-level display modes (GRIDAREA, MATRIXAREA, SCANLINE, SCANPOINT).
tldr.outcome: The proposal sought community feedback on whether these modes should be included in the developing Network Graphics Protocol.

today: This RFC is an early proposal from 1971 for the Network Graphics Protocol. It represents thinking on how to support both vector and raster graphics over a network at a time when computer graphics was still a specialized and diverse field with many different display technologies.

sections.title: The Illinois Graphics System
sections.content:
The University of Illinois' Center for Advanced Computation was not simply connecting an existing computer center to the ARPANET. Instead, it was building a complete computer system from scratch, specifically to use the ILLIAC IV supercomputer and the network. Unlike other ARPANET sites, Illinois had the rare chance to design its graphics system to be network-compatible from the start, rather than adapting an existing system.

The RFC outlines the display types the Illinois team wanted to support and proposes which ones should be part of the emerging Network Graphics Protocol. The document is framed as a request for community feedback from other ARPANET nodes about what display modes they needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A college with a big new computer was building its picture-drawing system, and it asked the network what modes everyone should support.

sections.title: Standard Display Elements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies eight types of display operations needed in a graphics protocol: Points (marking locations, optionally with a symbol or intensity level); Lines and Vectors (two-point lines versus vectors from current position); Character Streams (text labels on drawings); Viewport and Window specifications (for displaying scaled or translated views); Instance Transformations (reusing graphical patterns); Equipment-Specific Byte Streams (sending raw commands to specialized hardware); and Input Readback (keyboard and function button presses, cursor positions, light-pen hits).

The RFC notes that the protocol must support both vector devices (plotters, storage displays like CalComp and Adage) and raster devices (electrostatic printers, line printers, and devices with grey-level capability).
sections.plainLanguage: A graphics system needs to draw dots and lines, write text, zoom in and out, reuse patterns, send special commands to equipment, and let users click and type.

sections.title: Grey-Level Display Modes
sections.content:
The RFC proposes four specialized display modes for grey-scale and raster devices: GRIDAREA sets up an I-by-J grid with a specified number of intensity levels, then fills individual grid cells with intensity values. MATRIXAREA treats the display as a raster of dot-matrix characters, allowing the user to define custom pseudo-character sets and fill the display left-to-right, top-to-bottom like a line printer. SCANLINE scans across the display at a constant step size, and the user specifies only the X locations where intensity changes and what the new intensity should be. SCANPOINT is similar but simpler: the scan position is handled automatically, and the user supplies only the intensity level for each point.

The RFC notes that SCANLINE is already implemented in hardware on the Coordinated Science Laboratory display at the University. The four modes are designed to efficiently encode grey-scale images for transmission and display.
sections.plainLanguage: For shaded pictures, the system can fill a grid with grey levels, or use dot patterns like a printer, or scan lines while changing darkness, or just say the darkness of each point.

references.text: Kelley, K., "Proposed Graphic Display Modes", RFC 184, July 1971.
